subject: Discovery recap: Finly — p95 latency / streaming UX / concurrency
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
To: Sam Patel <sam.patel@finly.com>
Cc: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 10 Feb 2026 15:12:00 -0800
Subject: Discovery recap: Finly — p95 latency & concurrency targets

Hi Sam — thanks again for the call today. 

Quick recap from our side (capturing pain, goals, success criteria, next steps):

Pain points we heard
- p95 generation latency for short responses (~<256 tokens) is currently in the 800–1,200ms range; this negatively impacts your customer-facing chat UX.
- Streaming UX: long first-byte delays lead to spinners / perceived slowness even when total token generation is reasonable.
- Concurrency: the existing infra can’t sustain more than ~60 concurrent streams without severe degradation; you need sustained 100–120 concurrent real-time sessions and spikes to ~250.
- Cost: running with current autoscaling results in unpredictable unit costs for peak periods.

Current stack (as discussed)
- Prototype uses a managed LLM provider for evals; production is an on-prem/self-hosted Triton + custom HTTP layer (8x A10 equivalent) for inference.
- Frontend uses streaming via SSE; you’ve seen inconsistent first-byte timing across requests.

Success criteria (what Finly said success looks like)
- p95 token latency <= 350ms for <256 token responses under target concurrency.
- First-byte (streaming) latency consistently < 150ms for interactive flows.
- Sustained 100–120 concurrent streams with graceful degradation to 250 burst.
- No perceptible UX stalls (smooth token stream for the end-user).

Proposed next steps
1) SE deep-dive / architecture review (Aditya) — collect sample payloads and trace logs to reproduce in our test harness.
2) Baseline perf run: Redwood will run a controlled benchmark against a representative model/profile to measure p95 and streaming first-byte under staged concurrency.
3) PoC plan & success metrics: agree on payloads, token lengths, and traffic shape.
4) Follow-up: schedule a 60-minute technical deep-dive next week to confirm configs and run first smoke tests.

Requested from Finly
- 2–3 representative prompt examples (short, medium).
- Example traffic pattern (qps/concurrency over 24h and peak).
- Any infra constraints (on-prem-only, VPC limits, network egress windows).

I attached a short set of call notes for your reference (finly-call-notes.pdf).

If that aligns, I’ll loop in Aditya to coordinate the SE session and propose times.

Thanks —
Marissa Cole
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
marissa_cole@redwood.com | +1 415-555-0147

From: Sam Patel <sam.patel@finly.com>

Date: Tue, 10 Feb 2026 16:02:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Discovery recap: Finly — p95 latency & concurrency targets

Thanks Marissa — this is perfect and matches our notes. Couple clarifications from our side: 
- Targets: we can be flexible but would consider the project successful if p95 <= 400ms for responses <256 tokens (ideal 350ms).
- Streaming: first-byte target of <=150ms is accurate; if we can get the first token under 200ms consistently that would already be a big win.
- Concurrency: goal is 100 sustained concurrent sessions (typical business day) with the ability to handle 200–250 bursts for short periods.
- Current infra: we run inference on a private cloud (8x A100-equivalent) but network egress and NVLink topology limit some batching approaches.

I’ll pull together sample prompts and a 24h traffic export by EOD tomorrow. We’re happy to do the SE deep-dive — Wed or Thu next week works for our engineering team (afternoon PT).

On Wed 02/11, 1–3pm PT or Thu 02/12, 10–12pm PT would work.

Sam

From: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Discovery recap: Finly — Discovery deep-dive / proposed test plan

Hi Sam — thanks for the details and for offering sample payloads. I’m Aditya (SE) — quick technical notes + proposed plan so we come prepared for the deep-dive: 

Quick read on likely bottlenecks
- Batching at high concurrency can increase p95 for short responses; we’ll need to balance batching window vs latency.
- Streaming first-byte delays often stem from buffer sizes (server + client), TLS handshake timing, or model initialization stalls on cold KV cache hits.
- KV cache/prefix caching can reduce per-request compute when users have repeated context; we’ll want to measure cache hit ratio.

Proposed minimal benchmark config
- Model profile: 2k context, 256-token gen limit for interactive flows.
- Traffic shape: 100 sustained concurrency, 250 spike for 60s, average token length 120.
- Metrics: p95 generation latency, first-byte streaming latency, percent of requests hitting KV cache, CPU/GPU utilization, and tail queue lengths.
- Infra notes: we’ll test with Redwood runtime using 16-bit quantization path and streaming enabled, and compare against your current Triton setup.

Pre-reqs from Finly (action items)
- Provide 3 representative prompts + sample SSE client logs (first-byte timestamps).
- Provide a small set of traces (request_id + timings) for recent incidents that show spike behavior.

I attached a small baseline config snippet for our test runner (baseline-config.yaml) — this will let us run an apples-to-apples comparison.

Next: Marissa — can you confirm Wed 02/11 1:30–2:30pm PT for the SE deep-dive? I can block that and we’ll run through architecture + run an initial smoke profile.

Thanks —
Aditya Rao
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
